extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (metaphysics, philosophy of nature, natural philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for explaining natural phenomena in etiology and philosophy of nature: how to distinguish original forces, laws of nature, causes, and the proper scope of physical versus metaphysical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between original forces and particular manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Original forces (e.g., gravity, electricity) are 'original forces' that lie outside the chain of causes and effects; their particular manifestations occur in accordance with causality but the force itself is not the effect of a cause nor the cause of an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say 'gravity is the cause of a stone falling'; the cause of the particular event is the proximate circumstance (e.g., the nearness of the earth), not the original force. The force itself is 'immediate objectivity of will' and 'lies outside time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of nature as relation of Idea to form of manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature is 'the relation of the Idea to the form of its manifestation'—the form being time, space, and causality; it is the observed, invariable rule according to which a force appears under given conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laws of nature as 'un fait généralisé' (generalized facts). Once a law is learned from experience, the phenomenon may be accurately forecast whenever the conditions are fulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiology must seek causes of phenomena and identify conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiology's task is to seek out the causes of all phenomena in nature, i.e., the circumstances under which they invariably appear, and to refer diverse phenomena to the universal forces active in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Etiology should enumerate and compare phenomena, distinguish circumstances that produce a phenomenon, and indicate the conditions under which each force manifests itself (examples: galvanism in copper/zinc/acid, chemical reactions when reagents meet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate differences of force from differences of circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: One must correctly distinguish between a difference of the phenomenon which arises from a difference of the force, and one which results merely from a difference of the circumstances under which the force expresses itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against taking different expressions of the same force (under different circumstances) for different forces, and conversely against conflating manifestations of different original forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature appeal to 'original forces' (no lazy explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indolence and ignorance incline us to appeal too soon to original forces; doing so substitutes groundless forces for proper etiological explanation and is philosophically illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not explain phenomena by invoking mysterious quidities or occult qualities when causal/experimental conditions can be sought and described. The schoolmen's 'quidities' are given as an ironic anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: The will is not a cause for etiological explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics demands causes; the will (as the thing-in-itself) is never a cause in the etiological sense. Appealing to the will instead of giving a physical explanation is improper for etiology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the will as the metaphysical ground (immediate objectivity) that lies outside the principle of sufficient reason; but etiological explanations must stop at conditions and laws governing phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original forces as 'qualitas occulta' — where etiology stops
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal forces active in phenomena must remain, in physics, as 'qualitas occulta' (original forces) because etiological explanation ends where metaphysical explanation (the will) begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that there will be an ultimate, unexplained force-character for which etiology can provide only the conditions and laws of manifestation, not an inner ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete physics enumerates laws and forces exhaustively
rubrics_metrics.description: When physics has accurately defined, enumerated, and distinguished all universal forces and indicated their different effects under conditions, it will be complete; a 'complete enumeration of all the laws of nature' would be a complete register of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for thorough empirical description of laws as generalized facts; completeness consists in leaving no unknown force or unaccounted-for effect in unorganised nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce higher grades (organisms) to lower physical/chemical/mechanical forces
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error for natural science to seek to refer the higher grades of the objectification of will (organisms, life) to the lower (physical, chemical, mechanical) forces; organisms are not merely aggregates of lower phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explanatory reductionism that treats life as a freak combination of physical forces (criticism of Descartes, Atomists, Lamarck). Within limits, physical/chemical explanation may be useful, but it cannot account for the vital force or organism as a special Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept analogies and unity of plan across phenomena (search for fundamental type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the same will reveals itself in different Ideas, there is an inner relationship and 'analogy' among phenomena; in higher grades this appears as the 'unité de plan' or fundamental type recurring in comparative anatomy and elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogical reasoning to discover family likenesses (e.g., polarity as a pervasive type) but do not conflate distinct Ideas or reduce one to another. Comparative anatomy's search for the fundamental type is commended as a guiding principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize causes as 'occasional' for manifestation (Malebranche's doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every natural cause is only an occasional cause: causes give occasion for the manifestation of the one indivisible will (the thing-in-itself); they determine appearance 'in this place, at this time' but not the inner nature of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand causality's limitation: causes explain the particular temporal-spatial occurrence, not the ground of the force itself. This reconciles etiology with the metaphysical idea of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor: etiology vs. philosophy of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Etiology concerns the particular causes and conditions (the 'how' of manifestations); philosophy concerns the original forces themselves (the 'what'—the objectivity of will). Both perspectives are necessary and complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect etiology to supply metaphysical grounds; conversely, philosophy should not substitute metaphysical will where causal conditions are investigable. Use each method within its province.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence principle: higher Ideas arising from conflicts of lower phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When several phenomena of lower grades come into conflict over the same matter, a higher Idea may arise which prevails but incorporates analogues of the lower phenomena (e.g., ossification analogous to crystallisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the identity of underlying will to explain analogies and the emergence of more complex, higher-grade phenomena from interactions among lower forces—an argument against simple reduction.
